decision: the prefill cost is the tensor rate, not the weight bytes -- my own conclusion from the nsys trace was wrong, and one division would have caught it

The 1.65x rather than 2.0x is the non-tensor share of each kernel, not a healthy route. Upstream's MXFP8 runs at 79-85% of the FP8 peak against this port's NVFP4 A4 at 53-59% of its own, so the 8-bit path is the better-utilised one and the NVFP4 kernels have the headroom

decision: the prefill attribution is the ACTIVATION format first and the weight format second -- the activation format selects the tensor core route, and the earlier note named the weights
why: the note's section on the prefill cost attributes it to the weight formats' tensor rates, which this run shows is the second-order term: moving 32 of 512 uses to A8 cost -1.18%, moving all of them cost -47.6%
evidence: the 4090 Windows port's int8-prefill artifact doubles prefill (2,762 -> 5,830 tok/s at pp2048) by declaring an int8 activation route with byte-identical weights, against a baseline that runs A16. A4 is faster than A8 by about the same factor, in the same direction, for the same reason
result: the mechanism is corroborated from two directions and the port's shipped line is already at the fast end: A4 is the fastest route, and none of the quality levers measured here is free. The activation route should be named before the weight format in any future account of this cost

decision: the third tracked attn8-family recipe, and the acceptance discipline that keeps the evidence honest
why: a recipe that is not verified by its own path is a lookalike, and the finding would not be reproducible from the tree
evidence: both attn8 recipes reproduced their hand-written variants exactly: 4.648907 and 4.613442 with delta +0.000000, the same four domain values, the same format mixes and the same byte counts (19,681,456,132 and 23,576,645,636). The a8policy recipe is converting and scoring against 4.661317 and 18,946,875,396 bytes
result: the recipe is the evidence and the conversion is its acceptance test, which is stronger than a format-table unit test for this class of change

decision: the powered endpoint does NOT certify the effect, and the split shows why: AIME improves, GPQA is a measured null
why: the 60-question endpoint was marginal, and the protocol note's arithmetic said GPQA's 198 would put it past the ~213 the observed effect needs
evidence: GPQA-Diamond added to the same corpus (dataset id AI-ModelScope/gpqa_diamond, per EvalScope's own adapter; options left in dataset order so position bias cancels). 253 of 258 questions scored in both arms. Pooled difference -0.02134 nats (-1.87%), bootstrap CI [-0.05081, +0.00655] INCLUDING ZERO, P(mean>=0)=0.067, sign test 132/253 p=0.53, Wilcoxon z=-1.47. Split: aime25 -0.0858 (n=30, needs 69), aime26 -0.1382 (n=30, needs 39), gpqa_diamond +0.0069 (n=193)
result: the pooled figure does not certify anything, and the domain split is the finding rather than a power problem: GPQA's standard error is 0.0095 nats, so an effect the size of AIME's would have been detected several times over, and resolving its own effect would need 1,415 questions

decision: the GPQA null is saturation: the model already gives the correct option about 52% probability, so there is little room for a quantization difference to show
why: an unexplained null would be as weak as an unexplained result, and the mechanism had to be measured
evidence: mean answer NLL with the shipped line: gpqa_diamond 0.6495 over 20.7 answer tokens, aime25 2.6045 and aime26 2.8535 over 2.7. exp(-0.6495) is about 0.52 against exp(-2.6) about 0.07
result: the options are given, so a multiple-choice answer is nearly twice as likely per token as a free-form one despite being eight times longer. A quantization difference shows where the model is uncertain, and this format is not that. The finding is therefore domain-scoped: 3-5% better answer likelihood on free-form math, neutral on multiple-choice science at a resolution far finer than that

decision: this port's own FP8 KV costs 0.19% at 32K, an order of magnitude below the third-party figure, so the calibrated-scale lever is spent
why: the last unstarted unit of the playbook was the KV lever, whose first step needed no engine change: measure the port's own FP8-KV cost before pricing a change to accept calibrated scales
evidence: ninfer-perplexity on the shipped nvidia artifact, quick corpus, 261,167 tokens, context/stride 4096/2048 and 32768/16384, kv-dtype bf16 against fp8: 4K 4.386170 against 4.391526 (+0.122%), 32K 4.193074 against 4.201042 (+0.190%). Per domain at 32K the sign is not systematic: fp8 is better on chinese_reference and english_long_form, worse on english_reference and ninfer_code
result: the predicate set before the run was 1% or more to make an engine change worth pricing and under 0.3% to call the lever spent. 0.190% is spent. The external figure implies the format it was measured on costs about 3.3%, and the difference is structural rather than an artifact: this tree's FP8 KV is fp8-e4m3-r256 with kKvFp8QuantGroup = 256, a per-256-element scale plane, where that format has no comparable one

decision: the KV authority now carries a measurement where it previously carried only external sources
why: docs/research/kv-dtype-evidence.md answers the k8v4-versus-fp8 format question and says so itself: no figure in it was measured here
evidence: appended a MEASURED-HERE section with the 2x2, the per-domain breakdown, the structural reason for the gap, and the verdict against the pre-stated predicate
result: the note now supports active-work.md section 7's closure from a second direction, and it records that the capacity a quality recipe gives up is a capacity cost rather than one a KV-precision change can buy back

decision: on the maximin domain the recipe gains +15.9% acceptance, and the fixture-corpus figure of +77% was the outlier
why: the profile table is chosen by maximin -- 'the worst domain decides' -- and the matrix warns that code is the most favourable domain for speculation, so the bench figure could not be quoted as a lane figure
evidence: measured through the matrix on the shipped flags (dflash2, depth 7, vision, lm_head, ctx 262144): shipped nvidia code 251.3 tok/s / 43.5%, attn8 code 270.7 / 50.1%; shipped chinese 132.3 / 15.7%, attn8 chinese 139.2 / 18.2%. Two extremes agree closely: +15.2% on the most favourable and +15.9% on the least
result: no reversal, and the effect is not a domain artefact in either direction. A synthetic tiled corpus is more speculation-friendly than any real domain by about five times, which is why the bench read +77%. This is the fifth measurement this session to correct a number reported earlier

decision: the served context is not lost: both lanes report KV 262,144, and the recipe's cost comes out of free VRAM
why: the note's arithmetic said the variant gives up 5.14% of implied context, which would have been a serious cost on a lane whose purpose is long context
evidence: the matrix's own startup lines read 'KV 262,144' for both the shipped lane and the variant; free VRAM falls 2.27 -> 1.88 GiB on code and 2.56 -> 1.92 on chinese. The earlier figure was arithmetic on a text-only lane, not what the lane serves
result: the cost is ~0.4-0.6 GiB of free VRAM rather than context. The recipe is a net win on every axis the table selects by: perplexity, acceptance, decode, prefill inside the noise, and context unchanged

decision: the profile table's own figures are stale, and this run is the third value in three weeks
why: an adoption case stated against the table would add the recipe's gain to the lane's regression and attribute the sum to whichever the reader prefers
evidence: the table records 337.5 tok/s / 56.2% for the nvidia DFlash2 lane; this run reads 251.3 / 43.5% on code. The lane's own note already records 349.2/61.5% (2026-09-24) superseded by 337.5/56.2%, and this session's lane-regression note records the same drift
result: reported, not edited: the table is a separate item from the recipes, and this port's rule is that a stale document claim is a defect to report rather than to quietly update

decision: the published field splits 6-6 on this exact choice, and one publisher's numbers confirm the axis
why: the product decision needed to know what others who ship this model chose, and why
evidence: 22 published v3 artifacts tabulated. Six keep the source's FP8 attention/GDN (official nvfp4, d0xin, wallawalla47, CaptainArni, lyf, kvnxiao -- mostly importing rather than choosing) and six re-encode to NVFP4 (cometkim x2, kaushikvira, MirkoCovizzi, kybrcore, Ostfralla). cometkim's published comparison records that NVIDIA-sourced re-quantization improved PPL but cost MTP3 8.9-9.7% and DFlash2 4.1-4.2% acceptance, and that the NVFP4 drafter module cost 64.3% against 67.9%
result: nobody publishes the same-checkpoint A/B this port ran, and nobody ships an attention-only FP8 variant; cometkim's numbers are the same axis measured from the other side and they agree. The user-visible bottleneck in the tracker is TTFT and cache starvation, not decode quality -- which is the axis the recipes do not improve and the VRAM cost slightly worsens

decision: coverage: C=1 and the draft depths are covered; TTFT and cache had never been persisted
why: the question was whether every model has been measured at C=1 for TTFT, cache and the MTP/DFlash2 levels, and the answer had to come from the records rather than from recall
evidence: the matrix log holds 1,354 rows, all C=1 by construction (every lane ships --max-concurrency 1). MTP 1-5 is swept on all four shipped MTP lanes; DFlash2 1-15 on three of the four shipped DFlash2 lanes, nvfp4fullnoex having depth 7 only. No file or directory under bench/, profiles/ or temp names any of the campaign's 70 cases, and none names ttft
result: TTFT and cache behaviour have never been persisted. The tooling is complete -- 8 campaigns and 70 cases including cold-long-256k, shared-*, session-* and preemption-snapshot-{mtp,dflash2} -- and the one campaign that ran left no records, which is the failure mode AGENTS.md names: a measurement that decides a shipped setting has to outlive the session that took it

decision: the first persisted TTFT campaign: 32-40 ms for a short cold prompt, 9.47-9.53 s for 64K, and 46% of the long one is not prefill
why: TTFT is the axis the tracker's own users complain about, so it was the gap worth closing first
evidence: run_serve_ttft_campaign.py --case cold-short --case cold-long-64k on the shipped nvidia lane, persisted to profiles/bench/ttft-2026-10-08/ (22 files). cold-short 32.4 and 39.6 ms; cold-long-64k 9,470 and 9,529 ms for a 279,180-byte body, status constructed, 200, 27 bytes out
result: at this lane's measured ~12,500 tok/s prefill, 64K tokens is 5.1 s, so about 4.4 s -- 46% of the TTFT -- is prepare and queue rather than prefill. That is the same shape the tracker reports (23 s median TTFT from a 53-token eviction, 30-36 s agent-loop stalls) and it is now measurable with persisted evidence rather than from a scratch run

decision: the TTFT runner recorded passing runs as failures, and the cause was its own summary print
why: two of four samples in the first campaign were flagged as failures while both carried status=constructed, request_checks_passed=True and an empty failed_conditions list
evidence: run_serve_ttft.py:273 printed json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) to a cp1252 console and raised UnicodeEncodeError on a non-ASCII character -- after the run succeeded and before line 274 returned the tool's own verdict (0 for a constructed run with no failed conditions, 2 otherwise), so the crash turned a clean 0 into 1
result: fixed by dropping that argument, and verified both directions: the same case now completes with no failures.json and reads 34.9/37.7 ms against 32.4/39.6 ms before the fix. The systemic form was checked rather than assumed -- every other ensure_ascii=False writes to a file with encoding=utf-8 or to an HTTP body, so the print calls are the unsafe ones, and no tool under tools/ reconfigures stdout

decision: TTFT and cache coverage for the eight shipped lanes, at each lane's own shipped configuration
why: the audit found the axis had never been persisted, and the one campaign that ran measured the campaign's built-in profiles rather than any lane
evidence: run_serve_ttft_campaign.py takes --profile-config, so a per-lane run is possible; the serve arguments are parsed from the lane's own launcher (start_*.bat) rather than reconstructed, including the launcher's NINFER_CUDA_SYNC=blocking environment and its explicit --chat-template. The launcher says why: 'A harness that starts Serve has to start it this way too, or what it measures is not what ships'
result: five cases per lane -- cold-short and cold-long-64k for TTFT against prompt length, anonymous-hot-continuation and session-hot-continuation for cache behaviour, shared-sequential for shared-prefix reuse -- one sample each, persisted under profiles/bench/ttft-2026-10-08-lanes/<lane>/. The tool records profile_config, common_args and profile_args in its own summary, so the configuration travels with the figures. A lane that surprises gets repeated afterwards rather than all eight being sampled twice up front

decision: prefill is 99.4% of the 64K cold TTFT, not 54%; my 'about 4.4 s is prepare' was an extrapolation
why: the first persisted campaign's own records carry the phase split, and I had computed the split from a rate instead of reading it
evidence: report_serve_phases.py on the campaign's request logs: cold-long-64k, prompt 64,509, prefill 9,414.07 and 9,464.23 ms, prepare 22.62 and 38.99 ms, TTFT 9,468.89 and 9,527.83 ms -- prefill is 99.4% of TTFT and prepare 0.2-0.4%. cold-short: prefill 29.72/31.39 ms, prepare 0.94/0.21 ms, TTFT 31.60/39.24 ms
result: the ~12,500 tok/s I divided by is a pp2048 figure (attention-topology-2026-10-07.md: 12,541 tok/s on the a8policy arm, 6,576 on the shipped arm at pp2048), and the tree's own depth sweep shows the rate falling with depth (swift15-lane-measurement.md: 11,868 at 4k, 10,463, 6,468 at ~131k, 4,201 deeper). The measured rate here is 64,509/9.414 s = 6,853 tok/s, consistent with that decline. So the error was using a rate from one point on the depth axis at another point on it, not a wrong measurement -- and the consequence is that the tracker's TTFT complaint (23 s median, 98.5% recomputed tokens at a 72% cache hit rate) is a cache and recompute problem, which the running campaign's cache cases are the instrument for, not a prepare problem

decision: TTFT-adjacent records already existed on one lane; my 'never persisted anywhere' was wider than the search that produced it
why: I claimed the TTFT/cache axis had never been persisted, after searching for filenames containing 'ttft' and for the campaign's 70 case names
evidence: profiles/first_request/ (2026-10-02, QUASAR lane, from first_request_lane.py), profiles/warm_lane/ (2026-10-02, warm_lane_sweep.py: TTFT 57.4 ms at 18 tokens, 453 ms at 4,056, 517 ms at 4,727, 2.4 s at 20,208, prefill 8.6-9.8k tok/s) and profiles/shared_prefix/ (2026-10-03, check_shared_prefix_reuse.py: 3,275 of 3,282 tokens reused, 99.8%, TTFT 26.8 ms). None of those names contains 'ttft' and none is a campaign case name, so the search was right and the conclusion was too broad
result: what was actually missing is coverage ACROSS the eight lanes and the campaign's other ~65 cases (preemption, agent replay, vision, 256k, cancellation). The three instruments each measured one lane, and their records are the pre-existing baseline the lane campaign now extends

decision: startup time is a real axis and it is dominated by the volume the weights are read from: 5.1 s against 40 s
why: the lane campaign's serve logs showed 'engine ready | total 40.0s' where the first campaign's showed 5.1-5.5 s, and the difference was my own staging move to fix a disk-space failure
evidence: measured in the two campaigns' serve logs: C: staging reads 'weights ready | 15.3 GiB | 3.1s | 4.95 GiB/s' and 'engine ready | total 5.1-5.5s | CUDA sync spin'; D: staging reads 'weights ready | 17.2 GiB | 36.6-37.6s | 468-481 MiB/s' and 'engine ready | total 39.0-44.2s | CUDA sync blocking'. The artifact cache stage line records the copy: C:\AI\models\... -> D:\ninfer-temp\ninfer-artifacts\...
result: the lane figures are unaffected -- the campaign waits for readiness before sending, and the CUDA graphs are captured at startup -- so only wall time is inflated. But it is the first measurement of startup as an axis, and 5.1 s is a warm-page-cache figure, not a cold-disk one. For the remaining tranches the staging goes back to C: (46 GiB free after cleanup) with the cache cleared between lanes, since a 17.65 GiB copy costs ~3.5 s there against the ~37 s read from D:

decision: the a8policy recipe's prefill advantage reverses at depth: -47.6% at pp2048 becomes +63% prefill time at 64K, which contradicts what I proposed an hour ago
why: I told the user the -47.6% prefill finding 'sits directly on' the TTFT axis and would take a 64K cold prompt from ~9.5 s to ~5 s, and then measured it instead of leaving it as a projection
evidence: TTFT A/B on the nvidia lane's own serve args, arms interleaved and repeated: shipped nvidia at cold-long-64k (64,509 tokens) prefill 7,024.0 and 7,028.5 ms (9,184 and 9,178 tok/s); a8policy prefill 11,421.2 and 11,493.9 ms (5,648 and 5,612 tok/s), TTFT 11,476 and 11,534 ms against 7,074 and 7,069 ms. At cold-short (30 tokens) the two arms are indistinguishable -- prefill 46.0/43.6 against 47.9/46.8 ms -- so the penalty is specific to long prompts, not a broken artifact
result: The -47.6% was measured with ninfer_bench at pp2048 (docs/research/attention-topology-2026-10-07.md: 6,576 -> 12,541 tok/s); the serving route at 64,509 tokens reverses it. This is the second time in this session I applied a pp2048 rate at 64K -- the first was the 12,500 tok/s that produced the wrong '46% is prepare' claim. Whether the reversal is a property of the recipe or of the engine's A8 path lacking an optimized long-prefill kernel is NOT established by these records. The artifact measured here came from a prototype recipe under Temp\opencode\ (artifact_id 97800bc4...); the landed recipe's own build (a8policy_official, 6e7d469a...) is being measured before any conclusion is drawn

decision: on the landed recipes' own builds: a8policy costs 63% more 64K prefill, attn8 is prefill-neutral
why: the first A/B measured a prototype whose conversion report named a deleted temp recipe, so the artifact a decision would ship had to be measured before any conclusion
evidence: three arms, nvidia lane serve args, interleaved rounds, stage cleared between runs. 64K (64,509 tokens) prefill: shipped 7,176.8 and 7,021.9 ms (8,989 and 9,187 tok/s); a8policy_official 11,628.8 and 11,609.4 ms (5,547 and 5,557 tok/s); attn8_official 7,205.5 and 7,176.4 ms (8,953 and 8,989 tok/s). Cold-short (30 tokens) prefill is 44.3-47.6 ms on every arm
result: the prototype build showed 11,421.2/11,493.9 ms for the same case, so provenance is not the cause and the reversal is real. attn8 sits 0.0-2.6% off shipped, inside the 2.2% inter-round spread of the shipped arm itself, so it is neutral at 64K and not a TTFT cost. attn8's cold-short TTFT read 66.9 and 76.6 ms against shipped 47.6 and 50.9 ms while its prefill was identical, so that gap sits outside prefill and is NOT claimed from two samples. Decision shape: the a8policy trade is depth-dependent -- it buys decode and acceptance, which matter on short turns, and costs prefill, which dominates long prompts -- so a single number for it is wrong in both directions

decision: the shipped 262,144 ceiling is served on all eight lanes: 260,081 tokens, 66.9-68.4 s TTFT
why: every lane advertises --max-context 262144 and none had been served at it in a record
evidence: cold-long-256k on each lane's own serve args, one run per lane: prompt 260,081, outcome success, http 200, cache 0, output 17. TTFT 66.92 s (nvidia mtp4), 67.49 (swift dflash2), 67.73 (ninfer dflash2), 67.77 (nvidia dflash2), 67.84 (quasar mtp4), 68.10 (ninfer mtp4), 68.41 (quasar dflash2); prefill 66.73-68.19 s, so prefill is 99.6% of TTFT again; rate 3,814-3,898 tok/s
result: the depth curve now has five points -- 11,868 tok/s at 4k, 10,482 at 45k, 9,184 at 64.5k, 6,462 at 131k, 3,850 at 260k -- a 2.4x decay from 64K to 256K, which is why no TTFT figure here may be quoted without its depth. The first read of these records showed zeros because the diagnostics block was empty in this batch; the figures came from the request logs and the serve logs' own done lines

decision: the published per-lane VRAM figures are stale by about 1 GiB, in the direction that understates headroom
why: the 256K runs print the engine's own capacity line for each lane at the shipped configuration
evidence: measured: every DFlash2 lane reads 'runtime 10.6 GiB | free 2.64-2.71 GiB' and every MTP lane 'runtime 9.96 GiB | free 2.85-3.28 GiB' at --device-state-slots 1 and 1,127,444-byte bodies. profiles.py's note and the launcher headers say every DFlash2 lane reads 11.6 GiB and about 1.50 GiB free
result: the ~1.0 GiB difference matches the tiled saturation guard the tree describes returning ~1.35 GiB, so the recorded figures predate it. Reported rather than edited: the authority is profiles.py and the launcher headers, and changing a published figure needs its own measurement at the scope it claims, not a reading taken during another experiment. This is the same staleness already noted for the throughput table, now quantified

decision: preemption, replay and snapshot recovery work on all eight lanes, and a replay is device-local
why: these are the tracker's own symptoms -- 23 s median TTFT from an eviction, 30-36 s agent-loop stalls, 98.5% recomputed tokens at a 72% cache hit rate -- and none of the cases had ever been run
evidence: 40 case-runs (eight lanes x five cases): agent replay, agent snapshot, preemption replay, preemption snapshot, and the route-specific preemption snapshot. report.py's own required_mechanism_status reads observed for all 40 -- failed_conditions never covered this, and render.py says so: 'Required mechanisms do not change whether measured latency is retained'. preemption-replay replays 238-255 tokens in 65.5-75.7 ms and agent-continuation-replay 424-448 tokens in 130.0-150.6 ms, i.e. 0.26-0.34 ms/token. Snapshot cases move state 147-560 MiB d2h and 147-374 MiB h2d plus 8-36 MiB of KV
result: the replay cases move ZERO bytes d2h or h2d -- state d2h/h2d and kv d2h/h2d all read 0 -- so a replay recomputes from a device-resident checkpoint rather than round-tripping to host, while a snapshot restore does round-trip. Near-identical figures across all eight lanes (D2H 187 MiB on every lane, replay 65-76 ms) say these mechanisms are not lane-dependent, so the artifact and spec route buy nothing here and cost nothing. The tracker's symptom did not reproduce on any shipped lane at these cases. Case premises were preserved by merging the tool's profile args with the lane's spec route only, and verified before the run: preemption-replay kept --max-context 512 --kv-capacity 512 --no-prefix-reuse --host-context-mib 0

decision: vision works on all eight lanes and multimodal prefix reuse skips image preprocessing entirely
why: every lane ships --vision, and only one lane had ever been measured with media (swift15's lane doc); the media-* cases had never been run
evidence: 24 case-runs (eight lanes x media-cold-image, media-prefix-continuation, media-prefix-append), all success, no failed conditions, no error codes. Cold image (428-token prompt): vision phase 16.1-19.8 ms, prepare 32.9-42.3 ms, prefill 71.3-87.1 ms, TTFT 128.2-149.7 ms. Continuation of the same image (464 tokens, 441 reused): vision 0.0 ms on EVERY lane, TTFT 46.7-62.9 ms, path checkpoint. Append with a new suffix image (1,490 tokens, 441 reused): vision 43.3-45.1 ms -- the new image is preprocessed while the reused prefix is not -- TTFT 189.6-218.9 ms
result: the zero vision phase on the continuation is the proof that the media cache engages rather than the image being re-encoded: preprocessing is skipped, not hidden. As with preemption, the figures are near-identical across all eight lanes, so vision behaviour does not depend on the artifact or the spec route. The continuation's 46.7-62.9 ms sits on the fixed ~45 ms prefill cost identified in the cold/cache tranche, now seen from a third direction

decision: quality at depth: both candidates beat shipped at 4K and 64K, attn8 stably and a8policy by half as much at depth, while a8policy costs 45% more time per 64K window
why: all quality evidence so far was short-context, while the shipped window is 260K and the two candidates differ in attention precision -- where accumulated depth error shows first
evidence: ninfer-perplexity over eval/corpora/perplexity-1m/manifest.json, identical protocol per depth, three arms. 4K context (496 windows, 1,044,557 tokens): shipped 4.68676, attn8 4.64891 (-0.81%), a8policy 4.66132 (-0.54%). 64K context (16 windows, 1,044,557 tokens): shipped 4.43339, attn8 4.39967 (-0.76%), a8policy 4.42387 (-0.21%). Per-64K-window time: shipped 10.3 s, attn8 10.4-10.5 s, a8policy 15.0-15.1 s -- +45% over 16 windows (2m47.7s against 4m2.3s)
result: today's runs reproduce the earlier session's prototype figures to six significant figures (a8policy 4.661317 recorded vs 4.66132; attn8 4.648907 recorded vs 4.64891), so the landed recipes reproduce their prototypes and the prototype-vs-official gap seen in the first TTFT A/B was noise, not artifact identity. Decision shape, on everything measured today: attn8 dominates a8policy -- better quality at both depths, no 64K prefill penalty, TTFT-neutral, at +3.9% size -- while a8policy retains its claim on short-turn decode and acceptance from an earlier measurement that has NOT been re-verified on the serving route in this session

decision: closing the one shipped-lane gap in the draft axis: nvfp4fullnoex swept at every DFlash2 depth
why: the coverage audit found this lane's depth 7 resting on a single point while its three sibling DFlash2 lanes (quasar, swift15, nvidia) each have the full 1-15 measured; it is the only remaining gap on the axis the original question named
evidence: v3_profile_matrix.py widths --art nvfp4fullnoex --spec dflash2 --all-widths --vision --domain code --rounds 3, which is exactly the configuration the siblings used, read from matrix_v3.jsonl rather than from the tool's help: domain=code, max_context=262144, vision=True, sampling=documented, three rounds per depth, tags of the form nvfp4fullnoex-v3-dflash2-d<N>-vision-ctx262144
result: the siblings' sweeps are not flat, so this is not a formality: quasar's code-domain decode rises 151.5 / 196.4 / 231.1 / 268.1 / 288.6 / 323.6 / 325.2 tok/s at depths 1-7 and continues to 408-418 at depth 15, meaning depth 7 is not the code-domain maximum for that artifact and the shipped choice must rest on something else -- the maximin rule across domains, or acceptance, or the quality of longer drafts. Whether nvfp4fullnoex shows the same shape is the question; if it does, the lane's depth 7 deserves the same re-examination the siblings had

decision: the nvfp4fullnoex depth axis is swept 1-15, and it is the only self-consistent full-depth record any lane has: acceptance falls from 0.843 at depth 1 to 0.235 at depth 15
why: the lane's shipped depth 7 rested on a single point while its three siblings had the full sweep
result: decode tracks acceptance -- the non-monotone shape (a dip at d8, a peak at d9) is the acceptance curve, not instrument noise, since both move together. Depth 7 is defensible; depth 9 reads 23% faster on code alone at accept 0.567, but code is the most favourable domain in this port's own record, so the shipped choice can only be judged across domains -- the check the siblings got.

decision: every pre-existing matrix row describes a superseded artifact revision: the depth-7 rows disagree at 0.4873 and 0.6298 acceptance because the digest changed, not because the card drifted
why: the new depth-7 samples read 305-353 tok/s against the older 279-297 at the same tag, and I was about to attribute the split to this card's clock windows -- which is what the port's rules say to expect
evidence: the rows carry digest and digest_tokens for exactly this. nvfp4fullnoex depth 7 code: seven older rows digest e7e70b690330f08f / 1,561 tokens / accept 0.4873 / runtime 11.6 GiB, four rows today digest cc88a2c294f612f4 / 1,551 tokens / accept 0.6298 / runtime 10.6 GiB. Acceptance is a ratio of speculative decisions, so it cannot move with clock drift at all, which is the tell that should have stopped the clock explanation before the digest did
result: so the September sweeps for quasar, swift15 and nvidia describe earlier revisions of their artifacts and their decode/acceptance figures are not comparable with anything measured today; only their shape is. Today's nvfp4fullnoex sweep is the only full-depth record taken against a current artifact in one session. Re-sweeping the other three lanes against the current artifacts is now a named, bounded task rather than an untested assumption

decision: my digest-based claim that the pre-existing matrix rows describe a superseded artifact does not hold: sampling is stochastic, so digests cannot discriminate
why: I read a digest change at identical tag as proof of an artifact revision and wrote that into the trail, and the acceptance difference (0.4873 against 0.6298) as corroboration
evidence: v3_profile_matrix.py's DOCUMENTED_SAMPLING is temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20 -- the model card's thinking-mode set -- so output text, and therefore the digest and the acceptance of any given draft, vary run to run by construction. Measured: 35 of 295 full-configuration keys produced more than one digest, which is exactly what temperature 1.0 predicts and is not evidence of anything
result: what DOES discriminate a build is memory, which is not stochastic: 37 keys report more than one runtime_gib, e.g. nvfp4fullnoex dflash2 d7 code vision at 11.6 against 10.6 GiB, matching the tiled saturation guard the tree describes. decision: the prefill kernel profile is VOID: the two arms collided on one port and I killed the profiler instead of the serve, so neither trace describes the request it claims
why: I ran an nsys profile to attribute the prefill decay and was one step from reporting its kernel shares
evidence: the 8k arm's kernel table reports 39,058.9 ms of kernel time for a request whose traced wall time was 3.4 s and whose untraced prefill was 510 ms; the 64k arm reports 1,511.1 ms of kernel time for a prefill measured at about 6,700 ms, with FEWER instances of the same kernels than the 8k arm (688 -> 192 for nvfp4_a4_mma_kernel), which is backwards for 8.4x the tokens. Two ninfer-serve processes were found alive afterwards, both wrapping a profiler
result: cause: my harness launched nsys as the Popen process and then terminated THAT, which is the skill's lesson 8 exactly -- it kills the profiler rather than the profiled process, and here it also left the serve alive holding port 18099, so the second arm's request went to the first arm's serve and the second trace captured a process that never received its request. Fix, for the re-run: one port per arm, stop the SERVE and leave nsys to finalise (or let nsys stop itself with --duration), and sanity-check every kernel total against the request's measured wall time before reading anything out of it. Also confirmed the hard way: nsys writes a box-drawn table, not whitespace-separated columns, and --force-export must be given explicitly or a stale .sqlite is reused

decision: prefill cost is c/n + a + b*n: 45.94 ms floor, 54.66 ns/token linear, 0.7596 ns/token^2 quadratic, validated out of sample at 260K within 2.8%
why: the nsys profile of the decay came back void, so the attribution had to come from the engine's own timings, and the shape of the curve answers the question a per-kernel profile was wanted for
evidence: t(n)/n = c/n + a + b*n fitted to the lane configuration's own prefill timings at 30, 7,680 and 64,509 tokens and checked out of sample at 260,081: c = 45.94 ms, a = 54.66 ns/token (18,296 tok/s), b = 0.7596 ns/token^2. The three fitted points are exact to 0.0% and the out-of-sample point lands within -2.8%, an 8,000x extrapolation past the smallest fitted depth
result: the decay is the quadratic (attention) term and the crossover is near 70K tokens: the quadratic share of the marginal per-token cost is 0% at 30 tokens, 9.6% at 7,680, 47.3% at 64,509 and 78.3% at 260,081, where attention costs 3.6x the dense work per token (197.6 against 54.7 ns/token). Two consequences: the fixed floor and the decay are the two ends of ONE curve rather than two unrelated findings, and the target for any long-context fix is the attention kernel, not scheduling, chunking or the quantisation path -- all of which the flag work already cleared. It also bounds the product claim: conversations below about 70K tokens sit in the linear regime at roughly 16,500 tok/s, so the quadratic penalty is a long-conversation phenomenon rather than a general one. The floor's CAUSE (allocation against restore) is still open -- the model gives its size, not its mechanism -- and the kernel-level confirmation of the quadratic term is open too, with the corrected harness in profiles/nsys/prefill-decay-2026-10-08/VOID.md

decision: a8policy's prefill penalty is its linear term at 2.20x -- the A8 dense epilogue -- while its attention term matches shipped and its floor is slightly better
why: the recipe's +61-63% at 64K had been measured but not attributed, and whether it was the recipe's economics or an engine kernel gap decides if the A8 work has a future
evidence: the same three-term fit applied to the a8policy_official artifact at the lane's configuration, depths 30 / 7,680 / 64,509 tokens: floor c 42.25 ms against shipped 45.94 (ratio 0.92), linear a 120.08 ns/token against 54.66 (2.20x), quadratic b 0.7358 against 0.7596 (0.97). Modelled prefill: 30 tokens -3.6%, 7,680 tokens +97.4%, 64,509 tokens +61.2% -- all three against measured values
result: so the +61-63% is entirely the LINEAR term: the A8 activation path on dense projections costs 2.20x per token, while its attention term is indistinguishable from shipped (0.97) and its per-request floor is if anything slightly better. That rules out two candidate explanations -- attention with A8 activations, and per-request mapping work -- and localises the cost to the dense epilogue, which is engine kernel territory rather than the recipe's weights or its topology. It also means the penalty is on the COMMON path, not just long context: the model puts it at +97% by 7,680 tokens, which is a typical conversation rather than an extreme one. Not established, and worth saying plainly: whether a 2.20x linear cost is a fixable kernel gap or the inherent price of moving 8-bit activations where the A4 path moves 4-bit ones. The measurement localises the cost; it does not classify it. If the A8 epilogue were brought to parity the recipe would be a gain on quality, acceptance and decode at no prefill cost, which makes this the first engine target with a model-side payoff attached

decision: attn8's throughput half reverses the adoption case: -18% decode and -34% acceptance against a -0.8% PPL gain
why: the adoption decision had quality, TTFT and size measured but not acceptance or decode, which is the half that decides it for a product whose experience is decode speed
evidence: ninfer_bench --weights <artifact> --spec dflash2 --draft-tokens 7 --lm-head-draft --kv-dtype fp8 --prefill-chunk 8192 --max-ctx 262144 -p 512,4096 -n 128, arms interleaved over two rounds on one corpus. Shipped: pp512 11,716.28 t/s, pp4096 15,619.69 t/s, tg128 decode 129.25 t/s, spec acc 0.1290322581. attn8_official: pp512 11,350.81 / 11,229.51, pp4096 15,192.75 / 14,793.19, tg128 106.41 / 104.77, spec acc 0.08499095841 in both rounds. So prefill -2.7 to -5.3%, decode -17.7 to -18.9%, acceptance -34%, size +3.9%
result: the bench is deterministic -- attn8's acceptance reads identically to eight decimals in both rounds -- so the difference is real and not sampling. The mechanism is coherent: the DFlash2 draft companion was aligned with an NVFP4-attention target, and moving the target's attention to FP8 shifts its distribution away from the draft, so fewer drafted tokens are accepted and decode falls with them. That means attn8 buys -0.76/-0.81% PPL with -18% decode, -34% acceptance and +3.9% size, which is the wrong trade for a product whose experience is decode speed. Recommendation therefore REVERSES: do not adopt attn8 for the NVIDIA lane on this evidence, and if the option is kept open the next check is the serving route's own per-domain matrix rather than the bench corpus, since the bench corpus is synthetic and its absolute acceptance (0.085-0.129) is far below the real domains' 0.44-0.55

decision: attn8's throughput is UNRESOLVED, not reversed: a third protocol gives +77% where today's gives -34%, and the two bench protocols both differ from the regime the lanes serve in
why: I concluded from a single deterministic bench run that attn8 costs 18% decode, and the recipe's own docstring carries the opposite sign from a different protocol
evidence: three measurements of DFlash2 acceptance for the same artifact pair, in three regimes. Real-domain matrix (serve route, code and chinese, shipped): 0.44-0.55. The recipe docstring's bench protocol (2026-10-08): shipped 0.1106, attn8 0.1957, i.e. +77% for attn8 and decode +24.4%. Today's bench protocol (tg128 after a one-token seed, -p 512,4096): shipped 0.1290, attn8 0.0850, i.e. -34% for attn8 and decode -18%. The shipped arm agrees within 17% across the last two; the attn8 arm differs by 2.3x between them
result: so my previous row's conclusion was as overstated as the adoption case it corrected: the bench does not settle attn8's throughput, it adds a third regime with a different answer. The likely cause is protocol -- tg128 measures 128 generated tokens after a ONE-token seed, so speculation runs with almost no context, which is not the regime the lanes serve in -- but that is a hypothesis, not a finding, and I have not tested it. What is established and reproducible: attn8's perplexity gain (-0.81% at 4K, -0.76% at 64K), its prefill cost (flat to -5.3% depending on protocol), and its +3.9% size. What is NOT established: whether it helps or hurts acceptance and decode where the product actually runs. Recommendation, therefore: do not adopt on this evidence, and the reason is unresolved rather than negative -- the resolving measurement is the serving route's own per-domain matrix on code and chinese, the two domains the retired probe has coverage for, where the shipped regime reads 0.44-0.55

decision: attn8 is REFUSED on its own measurement: -22.9% acceptance and -21% decode on real text, with zero noise on the statistic, against a -0.8% PPL gain
why: five earlier attempts could not resolve this -- two bench protocols sat at opposite extremes of predictability, three protocols disagreed, and the real-domain regime had never been measured
evidence: real text from the perplexity corpus, three fixed 12,000-character prompts, 512 generated tokens each, greedy so every arm generates identical text, the lane's own serve arguments, model id discovered per arm from /v1/models. Pooled acceptance: shipped 1170/2526 = 46.3% in BOTH rounds (decode 266.7 and 271.9 tok/s); attn8_official 1094/3062 = 35.7% in BOTH rounds (decode 212.5 and 212.0), i.e. -22.9% acceptance and -21% decode

The absolute level lands inside the 0.44-0.55 range the real-domain matrix reports, the criterion stated before the run. Three protocols now agree that attn8 costs acceptance and decode (bench tg128 -34%, this -23%), and the recipe docstring's +77% acceptance / +24.4% decode is the outlier its own protocol cannot be reconstructed to defend. Decision: DO NOT adopt attn8. Its quality gain is real and reproducible (-0.76% at 4K, -0.81% at 64K PPL) but it is bought with a fifth of the decode, on the axis this product's experience is made of. Mechanism now supported rather than hypothesised: moving the target's attention to FP8 shifts its distribution away from the draft that was aligned with the NV4 target, so fewer drafted tokens are accepted and decode follows. Limit stated: greedy acceptance is not temperature-1.0 acceptance; what is measured is the artifact's effect with sampling held fixed, which is the question. The harness lives in temp and must be promoted into the tree or it will be swept -- the numbers are recorded here and under profiles/bench/realtext-acceptance-2026-10-08/

decision: the ~45 ms prefill floor is capacity-INDEPENDENT: flat within 0.9 ms across a 32x capacity range, refuting my own '19.5 ms is capacity-linked'
why: the floor's mechanism was the open item, and the capacity hypothesis was the leading one from a two-point comparison
evidence: cold-short (30-token prompt, so the prefill is essentially all floor) at three capacities with every other flag held at the lane's own: 8,192 -> 43.74 ms at runtime 2.35 GiB; 65,536 -> 43.15 ms at 4.56 GiB; 262,144 -> 42.85 ms at 10.6 GiB. The whole movement across a 32x capacity range is -0.89 ms (-2.0%), so the floor is capacity-INDEPENDENT
result: this refutes the ~19.5 ms I had reported as capacity-linked, and the fault was mine rather than the measurement's: the small configuration I compared the lane against passed no `--spec` flags at all, so the two arms differed in the spec route as well as the capacity and I attributed the whole delta to the pool. Two variables, one conclusion -- the same shape as the pp2048-at-64K transfers earlier in this session, and the same shape as attributing a bench's numbers to a route it was not written for. What the two measurements TOGETHER do support, with each half now measured at a controlled configuration: a ~28 ms non-speculative floor (the small configuration's 28.08 ms, no --spec) plus ~15 ms of DFlash2 draft machinery (today's three arms, all with --spec dflash2, at 42.85-43.74 ms), with nothing capacity-linked. decision: the prefill floor is the prefix-reuse machinery at ~13-15 ms per request, after capacity, host context and the draft were each refuted by a controlled arm
why: the floor's mechanism was the last open item on the server side; two candidate explanations had already been advanced and both were wrong
evidence: cold-short at 262,144 capacity with the lane's own flags, one change per arm: as shipped 42.85 ms; no speculative backend 43.51; host context off 44.89; --no-prefix-reuse 29.86. The last arm agrees with an earlier session's 28.08 ms arm carrying the same flags to within 1.78 ms, so the flag is the difference. Capacity is flat within 0.89 ms across 32x, host context is -1.38 ms on against off, and the draft is -0.66 ms at 30 tokens where no speculative round runs

It is not the price of the feature in any useful sense -- the earlier warm-continuation data shows a request with 7,695 of 7,718 tokens reused paying the same ~44 ms of prefill for 23 new tokens, so the cost is per-request regardless of the reuse outcome. That makes it a bounded engine target with a measured prize: ~13-15 ms off the first token of every request, which on an agent loop is 13-15 ms per turn. Three hypotheses were refuted by controlled arms before this one (allocation/page-table work proportional to the pool, host-context pinning, and draft bookkeeping), and each refutation is the reason the answer is a measurement rather than the most plausible story. The remaining ~29 ms of non-reuse floor is itself unattributed

decision: the shipped set now has depth quality in one protocol, and its 4K ranking does not hold at 64K
why: the two remaining measurement-shaped items on the open list

decision: cross-path determinism holds: a cache-served repeat is byte-identical to a cold computed run
why: the two remaining measurement-shaped items on the open list
evidence: temperature 0, shipped lane flags (dflash2 d7, chunk 8192, two state slots, ctx 262,144), one 6,000-character real-text prompt: fresh process A's first request, fresh process B's first request, then the same prompt again in B, served from the prefix cache. All three returned 949 characters and are identical
result: cross-path determinism holds: the restored state produces byte-identical text to the computed state, which nothing previously asserted and no TTFT, cache or acceptance measurement could have shown. Two harness faults were found on the way and both are the same trap: the first run returned 0 characters on all three requests because the lane runs with thinking enabled and 128 output tokens were all reasoning, so message.content was empty and three empty strings compared 'identical' -- a degenerate comparison that reads as a pass. The fix is the campaign's own common args, --no-thinking --greedy. This is the third plausible-success of the same shape in this session (clean zeros from an empty diagnostics block, an nsys table whose totals exceeded its own wall time, and now three empty strings), and the lesson each time is the same: check that the artefact under test actually contains what the comparison assumes

decision: the C=1 queue contract holds (429 on overflow, verified), and both cancellation cases fail their own conditions without attribution
why: cancellation and queue behaviour at C=1 was the last coverage item with cases ready and never run
evidence: four cases on the campaign's own profiles (each premise lives in its profile), one lane's artifact, one sample each. pending-overflow: constructed, failed=0, nine requests whose outcomes are eight transport_error(200) from cancelled holders, one success(200) and one REJECTED(429) -- the bounded FIFO's overflow contract, verified. short-behind-long: constructed, failed=0, three successes. cancel-before-first and cancel-after-first: NOT_CONSTRUCTED, failed=1, outcomes transport_error(200) then success(200). None of the four declares mechanism requirements, so the tool's verdict table is empty and the outcomes are the evidence
result: two results of different kinds. The queue contract holds: a saturated lane rejects with 429 rather than queueing without bound, which is what pending-overflow asserts and what a user on a busy lane experiences. The cancellation cases do not construct -- their own conditions fail -- and I am NOT attributing that to the engine or to the case: the outcomes show a transport_error where the case expects something else, and whether the cancellation path changed or the expectation is now too strict needs the case's condition read, which this run did not do. Saying which it is would be the same guess-over-measurement this session has already had to correct three times. The next step is cheap and specific: read the condition these two cases assert and check it against what the engine now does on cancel

decision: the two cancellation cases fail on the runner's transport_cancelled flag, which never fires; the engine's cancellation behaviour passes every condition it controls
why: reading what the cases assert and what the run recorded, rather than leaving 'not_constructed' unattributed
evidence: both cancellation cases fail on one condition, with the same detail: expression 'cancelled.transport terminated by cancellation', detail 'outcome=transport_error, cancel_requested=True, transport_cancelled=False'. The runner's transport_cancelled flag is False on EVERY request of the run, including the eight cancelled holders in pending-overflow, which passes only because it does not assert that field. Everything the engine controls is right: cancel_requested True, outcome transport_error with http 200, the probe after the cancellation succeeds, and cancel-before-first's strict condition that the cancelled request have NO first output is satisfied (first_ns=None)
result: so the engine's cancellation behaviour is verified by the conditions that are observable (outcome, no-first-output, cancel-requested, lane-not-wedged) and the two 'failures' are a harness flag that never fires -- the inverse of an assertion that cannot fail: a guard that cannot pass, so the case reports not_constructed however correct the engine is. Two things follow. First, this is a port tooling finding rather than an engine defect, and it should be recorded as such: the cancellation cases have never run before, so nothing regressed; they were simply never green. Second, the one question not settled here is WHY the flag is dead -- whether the runner's classification misses this shape or whether the field means something narrower than the case assumes -- and that is a cheap read of the runner's cancellation classification, not a measurement. Until it is settled the honest status of cancellation coverage is: verified by four conditions, under-asserted by a fifth

decision: the 13-15 ms is gated by --no-prefix-reuse, but the mechanism is NOT located: the candidate search and prune are both refuted by reading
why: the earlier row named 'the prefix-reuse machinery' as the mechanism, which is a measurement plus a label rather than a located cost
evidence: codegraph on the per-request path in src/runtime/engine/context_cache/resource_manager.h: `candidates` opens with `prune(program)` and its search body is guarded by `if (enabled_)`, so with an empty index -- a fresh process, a 30-token prompt -- the search executes nothing. Reading `prune` itself (resource_manager.h:922) shows it walks owners_, shared_ and waiting_, all of which are empty in a fresh process, so it is O(1) there
result: so neither the candidate search nor pruning can be the 13-15 ms, and the honest status of that cost is: measured, gated by a flag, not located. The next question is narrow and cheap -- what does --no-prefix-reuse actually gate? If it gates a bundle (capture, the checkpoint store, the context cache as a whole) rather than reuse alone, then 'the prefix-reuse machinery' is the wrong name for it and any optimisation aimed at reuse would miss. At the 262,144-token ceiling a 256 target gives 1,024 keys per split, about 16 pages, against the 62 the old buffer held. There is also no fixed-size page array to overrun: the device path computes page_offset = position & kPagedKVPageMask per position and indexes the KV storage directly through kv_cache_<dtype>_code_index(physical_page, ...), and '__shared__.*pages' returns zero hits in the causal-cache directory. Reproduction, with its limits stated: the reporters' shape (a growing conversation fed in chunks, MTP3, int8 KV, greedy, CUDA graphs on, stock qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4full.v3.ninfer) ran to a 125,478-token prompt; 111 request-log records; a real decode of 185/378 MTP draft rounds at a 125,506-token prompt (mtp accepted 185/378, 48.9%); server alive throughout, exit 0. result: closing the row as do-not-patch, with the evidence ranked by strength rather than by convenience. The code argument is the strong one: the offered patch cannot apply and the mechanism it fixes is absent, so there is nothing to port. decision: the mechanism behind the sign changes is drafter/target alignment, measured in this tree as the drafter's own encoding moving acceptance 54.8% to 58.0%, and the maximin rule runs on prompts that are not the served distribution
why: four acceptance tables across two variants and five prompt sets, which needed one explanation rather than five
evidence: Three sources and one local datum converge. Published guidance: drafts 'intrinsically aligned with the target model' (arXiv 2503.13565, where every draft level is a quantization of the target), 'the drafter learned to imitate the target's own internal trajectory' (vizuara), 'the draft should generally be quantized at least as aggressively as the target' (tech-insider), and 'if acceptance rate drops below 60%, suspect a draft model mismatch or a shift in input distribution' (thaki). Structural: _nvfp4_draft iterates only components named dflash/dflash2, so the drafter is quantized by a helper the variant recipes do not touch, while both attn8 and a8policy change the text stack that the drafter proposes for. That is the mechanism the sweep's sign changes are consistent with: the drafter stays where it was aligned and the target moves away from it by a context-dependent amount, rather than the target getting uniformly better or worse
result: why this is worth a row of its own: it turns four acceptance tables into one mechanism, and it predicts where a fix would have to be if a variant were ever wanted -- in the drafter's own alignment (its per-site precision, or a supplementary drafter such as the n-gram route upstream is considering in #234), not in the target's kernel or its prefill cost. decision: a commit's message under-describes its contents: d7cbd1db carries four units of work under the needle-variant subject, because four failed attempts had left their files staged
why: the port-delta gate blocked four commits; a failed commit does not unstage, so the first commit after the fix took the whole index. The commit is pushed, so the history stays and the record is corrected in the next commit's body instead
evidence: the four units d7cbd1db actually contains: the code-repository needle variant; the port-delta baseline re-recorded (the ratchet had drifted: 278 upstream-owned paths, review verdicts carried forward); five lanes adopting k8v4 under the stated bound with every depth re-read; the eval harness's coding suite and its smoke run; and the retro sweep's two gate checks plus the rules they earned
result: the rule the failure earned, in AGENTS.md: commit with explicit paths or reset the index between attempts, and confirm the file list in the commit rather than the exit code alone. It is the same shape as the existing rule about confirming a commit landed -- a successful-looking command that did something other than what was intended

decision: the chain deaths' mechanism is named: this shell's background commands run inside a Windows job object, and the escape from it is verified
why: online research pointed at job objects as the mechanism for a silent tree kill (no flush, no traceback), and the trigger for the two deaths stayed unreproduced -- so the mechanism was tested rather than cited
evidence: IsProcessInJob with argtypes/restype set (the first call omitted them and returned -1, the ctypes truncation this repository's notes warn about) reads in_job=True, err=0, inside a background command; CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB is ALLOWED there (a child started with it ran), which is the half that decides: a job that permits escape, or no job at all -- and the first reading settles it as 'in a job'. So a job close kills its members silently, which is the signature both deaths had, while the trigger that closed one twice remains unknown
result: the escape is applied where it is cheap: the SWE-style harness launches its build and test steps with CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB, guarded so a machine that forbids it falls back to the plain call, and re-verified with a validate-only run. The rule in AGENTS.md carries the mechanism, the signature and the escape, because 'the cause is unknown' is a worse thing to hand the next session than 'the cause is unknown, the mechanism is named, and the work can be made to outlive it'

decision: the harness's model path measured: a one-shot tool-less model hallucinates the repository, and the apply fallback is proven against a repairable diff
why: the last unrun piece of the SWE-style harness was its model variant, and the field's calibration (OpenHands-LM 32B at 37.2% Verified, with a scaffold) said what to expect
evidence: asked once over HTTP with no tools, the lane returned a 54-line diff for src/ops/linear_bf16_a16.cpp -- a path that does not exist here, with a fabricated index line -- and git apply correctly refused it; the tree restored clean. That is the task's shape, not the harness's: SWE-style work needs repository access, which is why the field's harnesses at this scale are agents. Separately, the apply fallback is proven in the state the harness uses: after the revert, a count-corrupted hunk gives plain apply 'corrupt patch' and --recount applies it; two earlier attempts at this proof were invalid (one corrupted the start line too, which --recount cannot fix, and one applied against HEAD where the fix is present)
result: so --lane's useful shape is an agent that can read the tree, and the one-shot path is kept as the cheap control it is. The fallback's scope is measured rather than assumed: counts, not start lines

decision: the chain deaths' leading mechanism is falsified: the job permits silent breakaway, so none of the dead processes was a job member, and no memory limit exists
why: the job theory came from research and was testable; the flags and one escape test settle it rather than leaving it cited
evidence: QueryInformationJobObject (with argtypes, after the first call returned -1 for want of them) reads LimitFlags=0x3000 = SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK + KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, JobMemoryLimit=0, ProcessMemoryLimit=0, ActiveProcessLimit=0. SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK means descendants born inside are not added to the job, so the driver and the smoke child were never members and a job close cannot have killed them; the memory-limit theory dies with the zero limits. The escape test then verified the mitigation end to end: a breakaway child slept 25 s past its spawner's job close and wrote its marker (started/survived, 25 s apart), so the escape works even though the mechanism it was meant to escape is not the cause
result: the trigger stays unreproduced with its candidate space narrowed: not a job close, not a memory limit, and two constructed probes of the failing sequence came back green. The defences stand on their own merits -- per-step logs, a step-start line, one long step per shell -- and the breakaway flag stays in the harness as prophylaxis, proven harmless by a validate-only run

decision: both model shapes for the SWE-style harness measured: the one-shot hallucinates the repository, the agent investigates and does not resolve
why: the harness's model path was the last unrun piece; the field's calibration (OpenHands-LM 32B at 37.2% Verified, with a scaffold) said what to expect and the two runs say what happened
evidence: one-shot over HTTP: a 54-line diff for src/ops/linear_bf16_a16.cpp -- a path that does not exist here, with a fabricated index line -- refused by git apply. Agent via the desktop's bundled opencode-cli (2.0.26; the PATH CLI is 1.18.4 and rejects the V2 config with 'Unrecognized keys: providers, media, snapshots'): it investigated (git status, git diff, a build), exited rc=0, and left no change on the instance's paths, so the harness reported 'nothing to score'
result: so --agent is the right shape and the local 27B, one prompt, does not resolve this C++/CUDA instance -- a negative with a visible shape, which is what the harness exists to produce. Also recorded against this session: the coding_sample lane's first start failed with cudaMallocHost out of memory because the agent run's lane was still serving -- the repo's own one-GPU-job rule, broken by leaving it up

decision: the coding suites are measured on the NVIDIA lane as it ships: humaneval 87.5%, live_code_bench pass@1 45.7%, longbench_v2 short 31.6% / medium 35.0% / long 0% (context-refused), mbpp refused for want of a sandbox
why: the coding suites were the open item; the run also tested three assumptions the config had made about limits, sandboxes and context
evidence: humaneval 35/40 = 87.5%; live_code_bench 215/470 = 45.7% over twelve subsets (45.0-50.0% each); longbench_v2 short 6/19 = 31.6%, medium 7/20 = 35.0%, long 0/19 with 17 of 19 refused on the engine's 262144 context cap, so the long split is a context result and not a capability one; mbpp failed with 'MBPP benchmark requires sandboxed code execution for safety reasons' and is removed from both suites -- this harness has no sandbox because its targets are trusted local models, and the field demotes MBPP in any case. `limit` is per SUBSET, not per dataset: the first run asked for 40 and delivered 470 live_code_bench samples in 93 minutes, so the multi-subset jobs now carry small limits. The run's longbench_v2 job also reported job_failed on '[WinError 5] Access is denied' -- the transient rename lock this repository's notes already record -- and its scores were read from the backend's own review files, which is the remedy those notes prescribe; 15 lines were truncated by the fault and skipped with a count
result: the scores are per-suite measurements on a shipped lane, not a leaderboard entry: humaneval is saturated and contaminated, and the honest comparators are the field's own numbers for other models on other benchmarks. What the run establishes is that the suites work end to end on this engine and what they measure here

decision: the ~45 ms prefill floor is the prompt's own chunk, and a separate Windows timer defect was costing every serve request 18-45 ms; the defect is fixed and the fix is measured against an interleaved control
why: the floor was the last open item in docs/research/lane-coverage-2026-10-08.md, and the timer component was invisible because it landed in three different fields under different names; the fix is a few lines in the port's own app
evidence: the floor decomposes as prefill ~= device_wait + program_submit (the engine's host_exposed breakdown): 17-34 ms of device wait plus 10-43 ms of host submission, with computed_prefill_tokens == prompt_tokens at 77/325/2575 and the same floor on dflash2 and mtp4. Ruled out one variable at a time: CUDA graphs (49.3 vs 45.6 ms), vision (46.4 vs 45.6), the draft backend (mtp4 43.7-45.2 vs dflash2 44.2-46.4), a fixed token count, and the prefix path (inverted: --no-prefix-reuse reads 117-163 ms). The quanta: initial_binding bimodal at 0.9 or 16.0-17.0 ms across 12 requests, queue_wait bunched 0-15 ms, total - prefill mean 28.5 ms; engine_core.h:2355's queue_cv_.wait_for(1 ms) has no predicate, so it resolves on the system timer, which is 15.625 ms in a process that never calls timeBeginPeriod. apps/serve/main.cpp now calls it, and the interleaved control (build-test's unpatched binary, 2026-10-09 21:38, same lane/artifact/requests) reads binding 16.1/16.1/15.5 with queue_wait 18.8/13.0/13.5/15.2/15.0 and total mean 77.3 ms against the patched flat 2.0-2.6, 0.0-5.6 and 56.3 ms; the mtp4 lane agrees (52.6-60.0 against 60.6-89.5). Fingerprint code cell 320.1 tok/s / 45.9% against the table's 322.9 / 45.9%, so decode and acceptance are unmoved
result: landed: the fix in the serve app with winmm linked, the probe as tools/bench/probe_prefill_floor.py, the closure in the research doc, a README runtime note and an AGENTS tooling row. Named gap: the CLI and perplexity apps run the same engine loop and do not raise the resolution. One unexplained transient recorded rather than carried: a single mtp4 run read 8.4/10.8 s prefill, not reproducible in a clean re-run minutes later (43.7-45.2 ms)

decision: the soak closes with no leak and no crash, and its verdict can now be had in minutes: a slope with a 95% interval on the engine's own exact counters replaces RSS, whose jitter was the only reason the run needed hours
why: the soak was the last instrument-ready item on the coverage list, and a four-hour loop is the wrong shape for a project that wants its measurements to gate work
evidence: 220 cycles of chunked context fill (125k tokens) plus a 2,048-token decode each, 5.5 h on the shipped QUASAR DFlash2 lane: host RSS 10,141 -> 10,187 MiB (+8.3 MiB/h whole-run, +0.2 MiB/h in the second half), device (system) flat to negative, lane answering /v1/models at the end. The run survived five hourly location evictions. New instrumentation: device_kv_used_pages and host_context_used_bytes read from /metrics every sample, per-cycle floors, OLS slope with its 95% interval; --selftest falsifies the estimator in both directions (flat -> [-0.1, +0.2], rising -> [+11.9, +12.2]); the parser was verified against the live lane (four gauges, host context 7.80 GiB of 8.00). Two corrections came with it: the eviction is opencode's known bug (anomalyco/opencode #51828 and siblings, twelve open PRs, none merged, no user-facing TTL), and the escape is detachment rather than console-freedom -- the 5.5-hour run carried consoles and survived, so the console is a separate hazard that tools/scripts/check_console_free.py guards
result: soak closed and recorded; the short gauge-soak (10 cycles, ~15 min) proves the new verdict path end to end; still open on the coverage list: the cancellation and queue cases, and cross-path determinism

decision: the proposal head is measured on all eight lanes on real text, and seven confirm the shipped setting while nvidia dflash2 loses 16.6%
why: ADR-0005 asks for a per-profile record and swift and nvidia had none. tools/bench/realtext_acceptance.py, greedy, two rounds per arm, the lane's own flags composed through profiles.launcher_args. nvidia dflash2: shipped 28.8% acceptance / 226.5 tok/s against 38.3% / 271.6 without the flag. The bench corpus could not answer it: it saturates at 0.9914, the tooling table's own warning. docs/research/proposal-head-per-lane-2026-10-10.md

decision: the first cancellation probe was void, and the request log said why
why: The abandoned prefill subject carried prefix_cache_hit_tokens 158447 and completed in 17 ms -- served from the prefix cache, so no materialization was ever in flight to abandon. The generation subject hit EOS after 50 tokens before the socket closed. Rewritten: distinct cold prompts per arm, and the verdict requires the subject to have no completion record at all. tools/bench/probe_cancellation.py

decision: under a background or detached launcher python's stdout does not reach a shell redirect
why: Measured both ways: profiles/bench/redirect-shell.log holds the shell's own echo, redirect-python.log is empty. A run that must leave a record has to write the file itself; this is why the A/B sweep's per-invocation logs were empty while every result.json was correct.

decision: the divisor sweep's transform reaches the artifact, and only the calibrated sites move
why: read_divisors.py on the shipped image and three arms: layer-0 GDN q/k/v/z read 53.4925 shipped, 213.9702 x4, 106.9851 x2, 26.7463 d2, while gdn/output and mlp/gate stay at 1075.2 and 836.0 in every arm -- the imported sites keep their own divisors. The seam was falsified separately in-process: patched load_calibration returns the scaled value and restores.

decision: the proposal-head finding reverses on the served protocol, and the flag stays on all eight lanes
why: The greedy arm (real text, temperature 0) read 28.8%/226.3 tok/s with --lm-head-draft and 38.3%/269.9 without on nvidia dflash2, which looked like a defect. Interleaved on lane_fingerprint.py's code cell at the served sampling: 329.5/323.6 tok/s and 45.9% acceptance with the flag against 257.2/257.9 and 35.9% without -- the opposite sign, 25-28% in the shipped setting's favour. The first comparison was between two full fingerprints two hours apart, the measure-A-then-B window failure this repo records. No profile setting changed; the per-profile record now exists for all eight lanes.

decision: a scripted profile flip ate the next field on every run
why: set_lm_head.py partitioned on the comma after the value and wrote back without it, so four runs left tools/release/profiles.py unparsable (ctx, kv_dtype, tok and acc gone from the NVIDIA DFlash2 line). The runs failed loudly -- four rc=1 and no measurement -- and the line was repaired from git show HEAD rather than from memory. The script now refuses a value that is not a bool and re-emits the comma.

decision: ninfer_topk_logprobs_test failed once inside the full suite and passes alone 5/5, so it is order- or concurrency-dependent and not baselined
why: In the first release-gate suite run (ctest --schedule-random -j 8, 2026-10-10 20:19) it reported 2147483647 indices and non-finite values, which is the op returning nothing. Alone it passes 1/1 and 5/5 under --repeat until-fail:5 (1.02 s each), and the gate's own fresh --no-cache run the same evening is green. It is NOT added to known_failures: that list is for by-construction failures, and excusing this one would hide a recurrence. The op is used by the scoring route (Engine::score_topk, apps/perplexity --topk-record), so a recurrence is worth attributing; the cause is not established here.

decision: the pre-commit hook checks the worktree while the commit records the index, so a release cut can land a tree the hook never saw
why: Found while cutting v1.2.0: the first cut staged dev's tree with git read-tree and then committed, while the gate edit sat unstaged in the worktree. The hook ran the gate from disk (corrected, exit 0), the commit recorded the index (the earlier, wrong-kind fix), and main's release commit therefore carried code the hook had not checked. Caught by reading git show HEAD:<path> after the commit rather than git status before it. Workaround applied here: git add the edited files explicitly, and check the index with git show :<path> before committing.

decision: I chained git tag after a commit twice without gating on its exit code, and both times tagged the wrong commit
why: The first time git merge --squash refused (main and dev have unrelated histories) and the tag landed on v1.1.0's release commit; the second time the port-delta gate failed the commit and the tag landed there again. Both tags were deleted with git tag -d before anything was pushed. The rule the repo already states is the fix: create the tag while on the release branch AND verify it -- git tag --points-at HEAD plus git rev-parse on both the tag and HEAD -- which is the check v1.1.0 never had and which v1.2.0 now passes.

decision: the A16 SwiGLU decomposition above T=16 exceeds its own profile's criterion, measured at 8.1e-3 against 6.3e-3
why: The route (LinearA16Post, src/ops/linear_swiglu/nvfp4/nvfp4_linear_swiglu_plan.cpp:40) is the port's own and had no oracle case above T=16. Extending the A16 profile to 17/32/64/129 fails at the same index at every extent: actual 4.59375 against reference 4.55671. Systematic, so it is the BF16 rounding of the projection before silu_mul. Reachable only at batch>=2 (T=(k+1)*batch), i.e. --max-concurrency > 1; every shipped lane runs 1. Cases reverted rather than committed red; reproduction in docs/active-work.md. Fix is a fused A16 kernel above T=16.

decision: a four-seam blast-radius review of this port own divergence found three criticals and thirteen warnings; eleven are fixed and five scheduled
why: Scope: the 278 recorded divergences (~13,000 lines against the upstream merge base), not upstream's own 700 changed files. Criticals: the A16 SwiGLU decomposition above T=16 exceeds its profile criterion (8.1e-3 against 6.3e-3, measured, disclosed, fix is a fused A16 kernel); verify_artifact --values projected 0.76 GiB while decoding a 12.64 GiB parent (fixed: refuses at 13.10 GiB); docs/serving.md advertised three tool_call_parse fields the JSONL never wrote (fixed). Warnings fixed: the ineffective SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE (three-arm bind probe), the console code page never restored (parent/child probe), the stale --prefill-chunk row, the mixed-format context_kv_materialize guard, the third settle-order site, alignas(64)+static_assert on the NVFP4 TMA descriptors, the atomic counters, inspect_diff --hash exiting 0 on differing payloads, tests/artifact in the hook, and the calibration acceptance claim rewritten to what is established. Scheduled: the inert FP8 MMA split-K path, the splice span comparison (needs a constructed counterexample), ngram_selection.h (a deletion that moves the suite size).

decision: my manifest edit put a double hyphen inside an XML comment and both builds failed at link
why: c1010070 Failed to load and parse the manifest, LNK1327. XML forbids -- inside a comment and the text I added had one. Found by a PowerShell [xml] parse of the file, which reproduces the linker error exactly and is now the check before touching that file. One occurrence, fixed; both trees then built clean.

decision: the fingerprint long-code cell prompt is a slice of a file this port edits, so its figures move with the code and not with the engine
why: My W2 edit to src/ops/linear/nvfp4/nvfp4_a4_tma.cuh sat inside the first 12,000 characters the long-code cell takes from that file, and the fingerprint then reported 14 drifts across six lanes (acceptance down 5 to 27 points). Not a regression: the code and long-chinese cells did not move, and code is a slice of a file the change did not touch. The note now lives beside CELL_SOURCES in lane_fingerprint.py: read a long-code drift against that file revision, and prefer code for a claim about a code change.

decision: the pre-flight test recomputed with the same filter the function used, so it agreed by construction
why: tests/convert/test_verify_artifact.py asserted projected == a recomputation carrying the same nvfp4-only filter. It could not see the gap that let a 0.76 GiB projection stand in front of a 12.64 GiB decode. Rewritten over every decoded format with the per-format cost stated, plus projected >= largest float32 parent: measured on the smallest artifact the old filter reads 0.66 GiB against 4.74 GiB, so the new assertion fails on the old code. A test that mirrors the implementation agrees with it whatever it does.

decision: the review split-K warning is a false positive for this tree, and the dead ngram selection surface is deleted
why: The FP8 MMA split-K block is unreachable here -- every schedule with kSplitWaveCtas > 0 is a TMA one and takes the other launcher, and no shape file carries a non-Windows arm -- but it is upstream shared source, so removing it would grow this port delta to delete code that is inert; the comment now says that, with the finding recorded. ngram_selection.h (284 lines) and its test (166 lines) had no production caller and the test called itself a control; both deleted with their registration, and the baseline size moved 157 -> 156 with the reason in its note. The incremental-encode splice now compares literal spans below the window as well, which declines a splice whose cached ids were computed under different spans.
